title: The tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9)
hook: one language, one tower, and a scattering into many peoples

segments.voice: Last week ended with brit: the covenant with every living thing, and the bow in the cloud. A new week starts on a plain.

It opens like the start of a fairy tale. In the old JPS translation: "And the whole earth was of one language and of one speech." People travel east and settle on a plain. Someone has an idea. Come, let's make bricks and bake them hard. Let's build a city, and a tower with its top in the heavens, and make a name for ourselves, so we won't be scattered over the face of the earth. So they build. Then comes a line that's almost funny. The tower is meant to reach heaven, and God has to come down to see it.
screen: `ONE LANGUAGE, ONE SPEECH.` → `LET US MAKE A NAME.` → `GOD COMES DOWN TO SEE IT.`

segments.voice: God confuses their language, so they can't understand each other, and scatters them over the earth. The building stops. The place is called Babel, the Torah says, because there God confused, in Hebrew balal, the language of all the earth. Babel is also the Hebrew name for Babylon, the great city, so the name itself is a pun. Here's the honest part. The Torah never says exactly what the builders did wrong. They don't kill anyone. They don't break a commandment. The sources are quiet, so readers have filled the silence in different ways. Some point to the words make us a name: a project to glorify themselves. Some point to lest we be scattered: God had told Noah's children to fill the earth, and they huddled together instead. One old midrash tells a haunting story. The tower grew so tall that carrying a brick to the top took a year. When a worker fell to his death, nobody stopped. When a brick fell, they sat down and wept, because it would take a year to replace. The building had become worth more than the builders. Some later commentators heard something else in one language and one speech: a world where everyone was made to say the very same words. On that reading, the scattering isn't only a punishment. It's a rescue. Many peoples, many languages, many ways of saying the same good morning. The world after Babel is noisier, and, they'd say, more human.
screen: `BALAL — TO CONFUSE.` · `THE TORAH NEVER NAMES THE SIN.` · `THE BRICK MATTERED MORE.` · `SCATTERING AS A RESCUE.` · then, large: `MANY TONGUES.`

segments.voice: Picture someone near you who speaks another language: a coworker, a neighbor, the family that runs the corner shop, a grandparent. If you know how to say hello, good morning or thank you in their language, say it silently to yourself; if you don't, sit with the wish to learn it. No tower, just one word across the gap.
Babel, the city whose very name means confusion, from the Hebrew balal. A city built to make a name, left unfinished, and a scattering into many peoples and many languages.
Your line: many tongues. The tower stayed unfinished; the languages all stayed. Day thirty-six, done.

howItsDone: Jews read the Babel story each autumn in the Torah portion Noach, and teachers often pair it with the midrash about the fallen brick to ask what a community values.

myth: the Torah spells out exactly what the builders did wrong
it never names the sin. readers point to making a name, refusing to scatter, or valuing bricks over people.
the tower was meant to reach heaven, and God came down to see it
the story almost smiles: the great tower is so small that God has to come down.
in the midrash, the builders wept when a worker fell
they wept for a fallen brick. a falling worker, they ignored.

fork.setup: you're on the plain of Shinar. everyone speaks one language, and someone says: let's build a tower to the heavens and make a name for ourselves. what happens?
options: God confuses their language and scatters them.
fork.reveal: God confuses their speech, the building stops, and they scatter across the earth. the unfinished city is named Babel.

original.note: Hebrew: Babel, also the name for Babylon. the Torah links it to balal, to confuse.

trapdoor: what you thought: people built a tall tower and got punished for pride.
what it means: the Torah never names the sin. readers see self-glory, huddling instead of filling the earth, or bricks valued over people.
what a scholar hears: a pun the verse makes itself: Babel, balal, confusion. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 24 weeps for the brick; the Netziv hears forced sameness in one speech.
guess: the city named for God confusing speech
the tallest tower in the ancient world
the first language everyone once spoke

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the "tallest building in Genesis" superlative; the closing judgment ("more human") now stays inside the commentators' reading; trapdoor drops the Akkadian 'gate of god' etymology (not in any cited source) for the pun the verse makes itself.
Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 11:1. Genesis 11:3–4 is paraphrased.
The fallen-brick story: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 24 (tower took a year to climb; they wept for bricks, not people). Confirm details.
'Some later commentators' reading one speech as enforced uniformity: the Netziv (Ha'amek Davar on 11:1) is the usual source. Confirm.
The Akkadian 'gate of god' etymology was removed from the trapdoor.
'God has to come down to see it' (11:5): midrash and Rashi comment on this; the script presents it as the story's irony.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
